title: RAW UNREVIEWED: prefix-quotient and short-word capacity for a genuinely nontrivial small letter code
summary: A source-free necessary-condition proposal for a fixed prefix-free letter code with at most22 entries, arbitrary finite lengths and possibly shared initial signs. Identity always survives; only a code actually using a multi-sign entry is at issue. Complete-word prefix quotients force further legal code strings and sometimes singleton entries. Two-sign whole remainders propagate non-singleton obligations backward; distinct second signs then yield a codebook-size lower bound. No native application, source values, solver, language or translation is supplied.

contract.A: A fixed finite working-unit alphabet, at most22 units in the contemplated application. Its native atomicity is an explicit assumption, not a manuscript conclusion.
contract.C: A fixed finite set of distinct nonempty code strings over A, prefix-free. Each represents a distinct source letter. Several codes may share a first working unit; lengths are arbitrary finite positive integers.
contract.W: Already bounded complete written groups. Each must be in C*, with source word boundaries preserved. No source word values or language are invented.
contract.K: The proposed human alphabet limit is |C|<=22, counting all entries. The necessary conditions below can conservatively count only demanded/used entries.
contract.nontriviality: At least one code of length>1 must actually occur in the unique parse of some w in W. An unused long code does not qualify.
exclusions: No empty code, contextual/state-dependent code, optional deletion, null padding, code crossing a complete-word boundary, or secret mode.
No claim that any derived remainder is an attested standalone native word.
No claim that a formal source-letter sequence is a grammatical source word.

human_purpose_and_cost.purpose: A short learned writing table may assign simple letters to one sign and some letters to fixed multi-sign spellings; ordinary open source words are spelled compositionally instead of receiving arbitrary whole-word addresses.
human_purpose_and_cost.writer: Given an agreed source alphabet and fixed table C, replace each source letter by its table entry and concatenate within the original source word.
human_purpose_and_cost.reader: Use the prefix-free table from left to right, recovering each source letter without a hidden code-boundary oracle.
human_purpose_and_cost.learning: Learn each source-letter/code pairing and every sign in its code. Total table size is not merely the number of entries; sum of code lengths and lookup effort are also paid. Ordinary language knowledge remains required.
human_purpose_and_cost.limits: This RAW is a capacity contract rather than a completed native or historical writer. Unknown names are spellable only over the agreed source alphabet. Extra source signs, punctuation, physical overwide-word continuation and any additional control alphabet remain outside the present contract and cannot be inserted to rescue its native application.

identity_objection.theorem: Every finite W over A is covered by the prefix-free identity table C=A.
identity_objection.consequence: No lower bound above |A| can apply to all such codebooks. A possible23-entry obstruction concerns ONLY the separately required actually-used multi-sign code. This distinction is part of the proposal, not an after-result change.
identity_objection.no_assumed_native_result: No native lower bound, including23, is asserted here.

quotient_theorem.statement: If u and v=u r are both in C*, then r is in C* for a prefix-free C.
quotient_theorem.proof: The complete decoding of u consists of a sequence of codewords. The decoding of v must use exactly those same initial codewords: at each step, two different possible codewords would be prefix-comparable, forbidden by prefix-freeness. Therefore the position immediately after u is a code boundary in v and the remaining r is a concatenation of complete codewords.
quotient_theorem.closure: Start R with W and repeatedly add every nonempty r such that u,v are in R and v=u r. All resulting strings lie in C* for any compatible C.
quotient_theorem.finiteness: Every added string is a suffix of an original word and is strictly shorter than the v that produced it. The distinct possible nonempty remainders are finite; no code-length cutoff or source dictionary is needed.
quotient_theorem.singleton: If the one-sign string g lies in R, g itself must be a codeword. Prefix-freeness then forbids every longer code beginning with g.
quotient_theorem.not_suffix_deletion: From u and r u in C* one may NOT generally infer r in C*. Example C={a,ba}: a and ba are legal, but b is not.
quotient_theorem.prefix_free_not_merely_UD: C={a,ab} is uniquely decodable, yet a and ab are legal while b is not. Thus this cancellation obligation must not be exported to every uniquely decodable/contextual code.

exact_constraint_reduction.P: Let P be the nonempty members of the fixed-point R having no proper nonempty prefix in R.
exact_constraint_reduction.prefix_free: P is prefix-free by its definition.
exact_constraint_reduction.factorization: Every r in R lies in P*: choose a shortest member of R that prefixes r. It belongs to P. If it is not all of r, quotient closure supplies a shorter suffix in R; continue by induction.
exact_constraint_reduction.equivalence: For every proposed prefix-free C, W subset C* iff P subset C*. Forward: P subset R subset C* by the quotient theorem. Reverse: W subset P*, so parsing every P-entry suffices.
exact_constraint_reduction.limit: P itself is an available formal prefix code for W, but may be far larger than22 entries and is not thereby a human alphabet or native decipherment. Its role here is an exact constraint reduction, not a free word dictionary.
exact_constraint_reduction.unbounded_size_corollary: If the singleton members of R include every working sign actually occurring in W, all used codes are singleton under EVERY compatible prefix-free codebook, regardless of size. Conversely, if some occurring sign is absent from those singleton remainders, P contains a multi-sign entry; as a derived boundary-aligned suffix it is used in a parse of an original word. Hence a nontrivial code exists when codebook size is unrestricted. The22-entry cap remains a separate problem.

definitions.H: The set of first signs of the nonempty strings in R.
definitions.F: The set of signs whose one-sign strings occur in R; F is a subset of H.
definitions.T: A directed edge a->b for each exactly two-sign string ab in R.
definitions.d_h: Number of distinct second signs among all strings in R beginning with h. For h in F, a one-sign remainder additionally forbids h being a multi-sign-code head.
definitions.candidate_g: The first sign of an actually used multi-sign code. It must occur somewhere in W, but need NOT be in H.
definitions.N_g: g and every predecessor reaching g along directed edges of T.

necessary_cardinality.base_bound: |C| >= |H|, because every required first sign needs at least one differently headed code.
necessary_cardinality.predecessor_rule: For ab in R, if a is a singleton code then b must also be a singleton code. Contrapositively, if b is not a singleton code, a is not one either. Since a prefix-free table with a multi-sign g-code cannot contain singleton g, every h in N_g is non-singleton.
necessary_cardinality.impossible_head: If N_g intersects F, the hypothesized used multi-sign head g is impossible.
necessary_cardinality.branch_rule: For each h in N_g, no singleton h is allowed. Two reached strings beginning with h but having different second signs require different h-headed codewords, however long those codes may be. Hence at least max(1,d_h) codes are required for that head; the1 also covers g outside H.
necessary_cardinality.bound: For any permitted g: |C| >= |K_g| + sum over h in N_g of (max(1,d_h)-1). Every member of N_g belongs to K_g: proper predecessors occur as first signs of two-sign remainders, while g was explicitly added.
necessary_cardinality.global_necessary_bound: Take the minimum of the bound across all possible used multi-sign heads g not already impossible. If no head remains, no used multi-sign code is possible. If that minimum exceeds22, the specified small nontrivial code family is excluded. A value<=22 is only NOT EXCLUDED, never a constructed code.
necessary_cardinality.missing_inner_boundary_caution: Considering only heads in H is incomplete: a used multi-sign code can begin after an unobserved earlier code inside a word. The g outside H cases must be retained.
necessary_cardinality.distinct_initial_corollary: If H already contains all22 working signs and |C|<=22, then exactly one code begins with each sign. The shared-initial family then reduces to the distinct-initial contract, independently of source-letter labels. No native claim that H has that size is made.

manual_toy_examples.name: Quotients force complete identity
deductions: a and ab force residual b.
a and ac force residual c.
The singleton codes a,b,c are forced; no longer code beginning with one of these signs is possible.
manual_toy_examples.conclusion: No actually used multi-sign code exists over this three-sign alphabet, even if more than three entries were allowed.

manual_toy_examples.name: Shared initials really permit a nontrivial code
manual_toy_examples.check: The codebook is prefix-free and covers all three whole strings; ba and bc share the same initial b. This is not a counterexample to a distinct-initial theorem, because it violates that premise.
manual_toy_examples.bound: With a used multi-sign b-code, two b branches are mandatory, plus singleton a: at least3 entries, attained by the displayed codebook.

manual_toy_examples.name: A sharp nontrivial lower bound exceeds the identity size
manual_toy_examples.proof: If either a or b is singleton, the complete two-sign words force the other singleton too, leaving no multi-sign code beginning with either sign. Therefore a nontrivial representation has neither singleton and all four two-sign words must each be a code. The minimum nontrivial size is exactly4, although the identity uses2.

manual_toy_examples.name: Conceptual23 is possible but not assumed for the manuscript
manual_toy_examples.construction: Take an invented22-sign alphabet, complete one-sign words for21 signs other than g, and the two complete words gx and gy with x!=y among those21.
manual_toy_examples.proof: Every nontrivial used code must begin g; gx and gy must be distinct whole codes. Therefore21 singleton entries plus2 g-headed entries are required, and that23-entry codebook achieves the bound. The identity22-entry code still covers the same words.
manual_toy_examples.warning: This is a mathematical teaching construction, not a native dataset or predicted native outcome.

retained_priors.relation: The reserved-prefix/direct-code architecture already motivates prefix segmentation. Its missing source table is not newly discovered. This proposal asks for necessary capacity of an arbitrary-length class before any source-value fit, not a new claim that prefix coding itself is novel.

The length1/2 CV code already used a global singleton-initial set and counted single plus observed double codes. That is the closest finite-length predecessor. The present quotient and branch implications remain necessary without a length1/2 restriction and without the old source grammar.

selection_boundary.smallest_action: If root independently selects this question, derive only replayable prefix-quotient and short-word/head certificates on a fixed already-admitted complete-word packet. No source dictionary, native value assignment or full code-fitting program is needed for the necessary bound.
selection_boundary.negative: A verified bound greater than22 or forced identity excludes only the declared nontrivial prefix-free, word-preserving, fixed-working-unit channel.
selection_boundary.positive: A bound at most22 leaves compatibility unresolved. It neither constructs a writer nor gives a phonetic alphabet, lexical meaning, language or historical identity.
selection_boundary.practical_limit: The class is only one plausible low-table orthography.
